newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: GUATEMALA BURIES SOCCER DEAD, DEMANDS EXPLANATIONS.
newsitem.headline: GUATEMALA BURIES SOCCER DEAD, DEMANDS EXPLANATIONS.

text.p: Funerals jammed the main cemetery in Guatemala on Friday as mostly poor Indian families buried their dead from a soccer stadium disaster in which as many as 82 people died beneath an avalanche of bodies.

Angry and confused over the cause of the country's worst-ever sports disaster, mourners and the public in general demanded better explanations from the government as to why the Wednesday World Cup qualifying game became a tragedy.

President Alvaro Arzu, in a solemn broadcast to the nation late on Thursday, pledged to find the cause of the deaths and named a high-level commission including the interior and health ministers to report back within 15 days.

"What really happened in the movement of such a huge crowd that filled the stadium to its limits? Who was to blame for the fact that our main sports field became the unworthy tomb of so many fans," newspaper Siglo Veintiuno askedl.
Convoys of black hearses ferried trampled bodies in tin coffins on Friday into the main Guatemala City cemetery, which was booked up for back-to-back burials all day.

On radio talk shows, in streets and taxis, in lines at the cemetery, authorities were blamed for slapdash security at the Mateo Flores stadium and the entry of hundreds of people with forged tickets who surged in unchecked.

"There are all these gangs and gangsters ... this happened because of the forgery of tickets," said Ana Hernandez, whose cousin Hugo Mendozaba, 41, was buried on Friday, leaving behind a widow and six children.

As more than 1,000 mourners, many weeping and looking drawn after a nightlong wake, crammed into the main cemetery, they tried to make sense of the fatal night. Mendozaba was overweight and was unable to escape from the crush. His young son, who was with him, wriggled away unhurt.
"The stadium is too small for this type of event. If only they could hold them in a bigger place, but Guatemala doesn't have one," Hernandez said.

Arzu's government has initially laid the blame on a "brawl" by rowdy fans in the upper terraces of the stadium, which has a 47,000 capacity but was filled far beyond that for the Guatemala-Costa Rica World Cup showdown.

Witnesses said gate-crashers pushing through an entrance at the top of the stadium overwhelmed fans below, causing a mass of people to tumble on top of each other. The entrance was at street level, with the playing fields and lower stands carved into a hill. Many died crushed against a chainlink fence seperating the stands from the playing field.

The exact death toll was still unclear. Interior Minister Rodolfo Mendoza said 80 people, all Guatemalans, died, but morgue officials said they received 78 corpses and another four had died in hospitals.

"The authorities were irresponsible, there's no doubt about it. At these games there is no security," said Anibal Pinon, 24, who mourned overnight in a Guatemala City funeral home for boyhood friends, brothers Carlos and Byron Barros.

In his first public address since he made a grief-choked appearance at the stadium on Wednesday night, Arzu acknowledged problems needed to be dealt with and appealed for national unity during a time of crisis. He announced that turnstile takings from the $7-a-head match would be offered as compensation to victims' families, most of whom are poor.

In a nationwide display of grief, flags flew at half-mast and government buildings were decked with large black ribbons. After suspending the game on Wednesday, Arzu declared three days of national mourning and followed it up with a two-day ban on sports activities.
Guatemala's soccer authorities faced possible sanctions from FIFA, world soccer's governing body, and were expecting to hear word by late on Friday.

The 40-year-old stadium where tragedy struck always fills with feverish crowds during big games. In Guatemala, as elsewhere in Central America, fanatical team followers sometimes urinate in cups that they throw on those below in one of the more outrageous of soccer's bizarre rituals.
